p: CRITIQUE OF THE GOTHA PROGRAMME
by Karl Marx
Translated from the German for the TIA archive, 2026
FOREWORD BY FREDERICK ENGELS (1891)

The manuscript printed here — the covering letter to Bracke as well as the critique of the draft programme — was sent to Bracke in 1875, shortly before the Gotha unity congress, to be passed on to Geib, Auer, Bebel and Liebknecht and afterwards returned to Marx. Since the Halle party congress has put the discussion of the Gotha Programme on the party's agenda, I believe I would be committing an act of suppression if I withheld from the public any longer this important — perhaps the most important — document bearing on that discussion.

But the manuscript has another and more far-reaching significance. Here, for the first time, Marx's attitude to the course Lassalle had taken from the moment he entered the agitation is set out clearly and firmly, both as regards Lassalle's economic principles and as regards his tactics.

The ruthless sharpness with which the draft programme is dissected here, the relentlessness with which the conclusions are stated and the weak points of the draft laid bare — none of this can give offence any longer, today, after fifteen years. Specific Lassalleans now survive only abroad, as isolated ruins, and at Halle the Gotha Programme was given up even by its own authors as thoroughly inadequate.

Nevertheless, in a few places where it made no difference to the substance, I have left out some sharp personal expressions and judgements and replaced them with dots. Marx himself would do the same if he were publishing the manuscript today. The language, violent in places, was provoked by two circumstances. In the first place, Marx and I were more closely bound up with the German movement than with any other; the decided step backwards shown in this draft programme was therefore bound to move us especially strongly. In the second place, at that time, barely two years after the Hague congress of the International, we were in the thick of our fight with Bakunin and his anarchists, who held us responsible for everything that happened in the labour movement in Germany; we therefore had to expect that the secret paternity of this programme, too, would be laid at our door. These considerations no longer apply, and with them goes the need for the passages in question.

A few sentences have also been indicated only by dots, for reasons connected with the press laws. Where I had to choose a milder expression, it is placed in square brackets. Otherwise the text is reproduced word for word.
London, 6 January 1891
Frederick Engels

Engels cut a handful of passages when he first published these notes in 1891, as he explains above. This translation follows Marx's own manuscript, so those passages are included here in full and there are no dots or square brackets.
LETTER TO WILHELM BRACKE
London, 5 May 1875
Dear Bracke,

When you have read the following critical marginal notes on the coalition programme, would you be so good as to pass them on for inspection to Geib and Auer, Bebel and Liebknecht. I am overloaded with work and already have to go far beyond the amount of work my doctor allows me. So it was by no means a “pleasure” to write such a long screed. It was necessary, however, so that the party friends for whom this communication is intended will not later misread the steps I shall have to take.

For after the unity congress has been held, Engels and I will publish a short statement to the effect that we stand entirely aloof from the said programme of principles and have nothing to do with it.

This is indispensable, because abroad the view is held — a view carefully fostered by the party's enemies, and a completely mistaken one — that we secretly direct the movement of the so-called Eisenach party from here. In a Russian pamphlet that appeared only recently, for example, Bakunin still holds me responsible not only for all the programmes, etc., of that party, but even for every step Liebknecht has taken since the day he began co-operating with the People's Party.
Apart from this, it is my duty not to give my recognition, even by diplomatic silence, to a programme which in my conviction is thoroughly objectionable and demoralising for the party.

Every step of real movement is more important than a dozen programmes. If, therefore, it was not possible — and the circumstances of the time did not permit it — to go beyond the Eisenach programme, one should simply have concluded an agreement for action against the common enemy. But when one draws up programmes of principles (instead of putting them off until a time when such things have been prepared by a longer period of common activity), one sets up before the whole world landmarks by which it measures how far the party movement has got.

The leaders of the Lassalleans came because circumstances forced them to. Had they been told from the outset that there would be no haggling over principles, they would have had to content themselves with a programme of action or a plan of organisation for common action. Instead of this, they are allowed to arrive armed with mandates, and these mandates are recognised on our side as binding, which means surrendering unconditionally to people who are themselves in need of help. To crown it all, they are holding a congress of their own before the congress of compromise, while our own party is holding its congress post festum. Evidently the aim was to conjure away all criticism and give our own party no chance to stop and think. We know how the mere fact of unification pleases the workers, but it is a mistake to believe that this momentary success has not been bought too dearly. In any case the programme is worthless, even apart from its canonisation of the Lassallean articles of faith.

I shall be sending you the last instalments of the French edition of Capital shortly. The progress of the printing was held up for a long time by a ban imposed by the French government. The thing will be finished this week or at the beginning of next. Did you receive the previous six instalments? Please also let me have the address of Bernhard Becker, to whom I must likewise send the last instalments.
The Volksstaat bookshop has peculiar manners. Up to this very moment, for example, I have not been sent a single copy of the reprint of the Cologne Communist Trial.
With best regards,
Yours, Karl Marx
MARGINAL NOTES ON THE PROGRAMME OF THE GERMAN WORKERS' PARTY · I

1. “Labour is the source of all wealth and all culture, and since useful labour is possible only in society and through society, the proceeds of labour belong undiminished, with equal right, to all members of society.”
First part of the paragraph: “Labour is the source of all wealth and all culture.”

Labour is not the source of all wealth. Nature is just as much the source of use-values (and it is surely of these that material wealth consists!) as labour, which is itself only the expression of a force of nature, human labour-power. That phrase is to be found in every children's primer, and it is correct in so far as it is taken for granted that labour is carried on with the objects and instruments that go with it. But a socialist programme cannot allow such bourgeois turns of phrase to pass over in silence the conditions that alone give them meaning. Only in so far as man from the very start behaves towards nature, the first source of all instruments and objects of labour, as its owner, and treats it as belonging to him, does his labour become a source of use-values, and therefore also of wealth. The bourgeois have very good reasons for crediting labour with supernatural creative power; for it follows precisely from the fact that labour is conditioned by nature that the man who possesses no other property than his labour-power must, in every condition of society and culture, be the slave of the other men who have made themselves the owners of the material conditions of labour. He can work only with their permission, and so can live only with their permission.
Let us now leave the sentence as it stands, or rather limps. What would one have expected as its conclusion? Obviously this:

“Since labour is the source of all wealth, no one in society can appropriate wealth except as the product of labour. If, therefore, he does not work himself, he lives on the labour of others and also acquires his culture at the expense of the labour of others.”
Instead of this, a second sentence is tacked on by means of the verbal screw “and since”, in order to draw a conclusion from it and not from the first.
Second part of the paragraph: “Useful labour is possible only in society and through society.”

According to the first sentence, labour was the source of all wealth and all culture, and so no society was possible without labour either. Now we learn, the other way round, that no “useful” labour is possible without society.

One could just as well have said that only in society can useless and even socially harmful labour become a way of earning a living, that only in society can one live by idleness, etc., etc. — in short, one could have copied out the whole of Rousseau.

And what is “useful” labour? Surely only labour that produces the useful effect intended. A savage — and man is a savage once he has ceased to be an ape — who kills an animal with a stone, who gathers fruit, etc., performs “useful” labour.
Thirdly, the conclusion: “And since useful labour is possible only in society and through society, the proceeds of labour belong undiminished, with equal right, to all members of society.”

A fine conclusion! If useful labour is possible only in society and through society, then the proceeds of labour belong to society — and only so much of them comes to the individual worker as is not needed to maintain the “condition” of labour, society.

In fact this proposition has been put forward at all times by the champions of whatever state of society existed at the time. First come the claims of the government and everything that clings to it, since it is the social organ for maintaining social order; then come the claims of the various kinds of private owners, since the various kinds of private property are the foundations of society, and so on. One sees that such hollow phrases can be twisted and turned any way one likes.
The first and second parts of the paragraph have some intelligible connection only in this wording:

“Labour becomes the source of wealth and culture only as social labour”, or, what is the same thing, “in and through society”. This proposition is indisputably correct, for although isolated labour (its material conditions being presupposed) can create use-values, it can create neither wealth nor culture.
But the other proposition is just as indisputable:

“In proportion as labour develops socially, and thereby becomes the source of wealth and culture, poverty and neglect develop on the side of the worker, and wealth and culture on the side of the non-worker.”

This is the law of all history up to now. What had to be done here, then, instead of making general phrases about “labour” and “society”, was to show concretely how in present-day capitalist society the material and other conditions have at last been created which enable the workers, and compel them, to break that historical curse.

In fact, however, the whole paragraph, botched in style and in content, is there only so as to inscribe the Lassallean catchword of the “undiminished proceeds of labour” as a slogan at the top of the party banner. I shall come back later to the “proceeds of labour”, “equal right”, etc., since the same thing comes up again in a somewhat different form.
2. “In present-day society the means of labour are the monopoly of the capitalist class; the resulting dependence of the working class is the cause of misery and servitude in all its forms.”
This sentence, borrowed from the Rules of the International, is wrong in this “improved” edition.

In present-day society the means of labour are the monopoly of the landowners (the monopoly of landed property is even the basis of the monopoly of capital) and of the capitalists. In the passage in question, the Rules of the International name neither the one class of monopolists nor the other. They speak of the “monopoly of the means of labour, that is, of the sources of life”; the addition “sources of life” shows clearly enough that the land is included among the means of labour.

The improvement was introduced because Lassalle, for reasons now generally known, attacked only the capitalist class, not the landowners. In England the capitalist is usually not even the owner of the land on which his factory stands.

3. “The emancipation of labour demands the elevation of the means of labour to the common property of society and the co-operative regulation of the total labour, with a just distribution of the proceeds of labour.”
“Elevation of the means of labour to common property”! This is presumably meant to say their “conversion into common property”. But that only in passing.

What are the “proceeds of labour”? The product of labour, or its value? And in the latter case, the total value of the product, or only that part of the value which labour has newly added to the value of the means of production used up?
“Proceeds of labour” is a loose notion that Lassalle has put in the place of definite economic concepts.
What is “just” distribution?

Do not the bourgeois assert that present-day distribution is “just”? And is it not, in fact, the only “just” distribution on the basis of the present-day mode of production? Are economic relations regulated by legal concepts, or do not, on the contrary, legal relations arise out of economic ones? Have not the socialist sectarians, too, the most varied notions about “just” distribution?

To find out what is to be understood on this occasion by the phrase “just distribution”, we must take the first paragraph together with this one. The latter presupposes a society in which “the means of labour are common property and the total labour is co-operatively regulated”, and from the first paragraph we learn that “the proceeds of labour belong undiminished, with equal right, to all members of society”. “To all members of society”? To those who do not work as well? What then becomes of the “undiminished proceeds of labour”? Only to the members of society who work? What then becomes of the “equal right” of all members of society?

But “all members of society” and “equal right” are obviously mere phrases. The heart of the matter is that in this communist society every worker is supposed to receive his “undiminished” Lassallean “proceeds of labour”.
If we first take the words “proceeds of labour” in the sense of the product of labour, then the co-operative proceeds of labour are the total social product.
From this there must now be deducted:
First, cover for the replacement of the means of production used up.
Secondly, an additional portion for the expansion of production.
Thirdly, a reserve or insurance fund against accidents, disruptions caused by natural events, etc.

These deductions from the “undiminished proceeds of labour” are an economic necessity, and their size is to be determined according to the means and forces available, partly by the calculation of probabilities, but they can in no way be calculated from justice.
There remains the other part of the total product, intended to serve as means of consumption. Before this comes to be divided among individuals, there is again deducted from it:
First, the general costs of administration not directly belonging to production.
This part will from the very outset be very considerably restricted in comparison with present-day society, and it diminishes in proportion as the new society develops.
Secondly, what is intended for the common satisfaction of needs, such as schools, health services, etc.
This part grows considerably from the very outset in comparison with present-day society, and it increases in proportion as the new society develops.
Thirdly, funds for those unable to work, etc., in short, for what today comes under so-called official poor relief.

Only now do we come to the “distribution” which the programme, under Lassallean influence, has narrow-mindedly in view to the exclusion of everything else, namely to that part of the means of consumption which is divided among the individual producers of the co-operative.

The “undiminished proceeds of labour” have meanwhile already turned on the quiet into “diminished” proceeds, although what the producer is deprived of in his capacity as a private individual benefits him, directly or indirectly, in his capacity as a member of society.
Just as the phrase “undiminished proceeds of labour” has disappeared, so now the phrase “proceeds of labour” disappears altogether.

Within the co-operative society based on common ownership of the means of production, the producers do not exchange their products; just as little does the labour spent on the products appear here as the value of these products, as a material property they possess, since now, in contrast to capitalist society, individual pieces of labour no longer exist as component parts of the total labour by a roundabout route, but directly. The words “proceeds of labour”, objectionable even today on account of their ambiguity, thus lose all meaning.

What we are dealing with here is a communist society, not as it has developed on its own foundations, but, on the contrary, just as it emerges from capitalist society; a society which is thus in every respect, economically, morally and intellectually, still marked with the birthmarks of the old society from whose womb it comes. Accordingly, the individual producer receives back from society — after the deductions — exactly what he gives to it. What he has given to it is his individual quantity of labour. For example, the social working day consists of the sum of the individual hours of work. The individual labour time of the individual producer is the part of the social working day that he has contributed, his share of it. He receives a certificate from society stating that he has furnished such and such an amount of labour (after deduction of his labour for the common funds), and with this certificate he draws from the social stock of means of consumption as much as costs the same amount of labour. The same quantity of labour that he has given to society in one form he receives back in another.

Here, obviously, the same principle prevails as that which regulates the exchange of commodities, in so far as this is an exchange of equal values. Content and form are changed, because under the changed circumstances no one can give anything except his labour, and because, on the other hand, nothing can pass into the ownership of individuals except individual means of consumption. But as far as the distribution of the latter among the individual producers is concerned, the same principle prevails as in the exchange of commodity equivalents: a given amount of labour in one form is exchanged for an equal amount of labour in another form.

Equal right here is therefore still — in principle — bourgeois right, although principle and practice are no longer at each other's throats, whereas in the exchange of commodities the exchange of equivalents exists only on the average and not in the individual case.

In spite of this advance, this equal right is still constantly burdened with a bourgeois limitation. The right of the producers is proportional to the labour they supply; the equality consists in the fact that measurement is made with an equal standard, labour. But one man is superior to another physically or mentally, and so supplies more labour in the same time, or can work for a longer time; and labour, to serve as a measure, must be defined by its duration or its intensity, otherwise it ceases to be a standard of measurement. This equal right is unequal right for unequal labour. It recognises no class differences, because everyone is only a worker like everyone else; but it tacitly recognises unequal individual endowment, and thus unequal productive capacity of the workers, as natural privileges. It is therefore a right of inequality, in its content, like every right. Right by its very nature can consist only in the application of an equal standard; but unequal individuals (and they would not be different individuals if they were not unequal) can be measured by an equal standard only in so far as they are brought under an equal point of view, are taken from one particular side only — for instance, in the present case, are regarded only as workers and nothing more is seen in them, everything else being disregarded. Further: one worker is married, another is not; one has more children than another, and so on and so forth. Thus, with an equal performance of labour, and hence an equal share in the social consumption fund, one will in fact receive more than another, one will be richer than another, and so on. To avoid all these defects, right would have to be unequal rather than equal.

But these defects are unavoidable in the first phase of communist society, as it has just emerged from capitalist society after long birth pangs. Right can never be higher than the economic structure of society and the cultural development conditioned by it.

In a higher phase of communist society, after the enslaving subordination of individuals to the division of labour has vanished, and with it the antithesis between mental and physical labour; after labour has become not only a means of life but itself the first need of life; after the productive forces have also grown with the all-round development of individuals, and all the springs of co-operative wealth flow more abundantly — only then can the narrow horizon of bourgeois right be left behind entirely, and society inscribe on its banners: From each according to his abilities, to each according to his needs!

I have dealt at greater length with the “undiminished proceeds of labour” on the one hand, and with “equal right” and “just distribution” on the other, in order to show what an offence it is, on the one hand, to try to force on our party once more, as dogmas, ideas which made sense at a certain time but have now become obsolete verbal rubbish, and, on the other hand, to twist the realistic outlook, which it cost so much effort to instil into the party but which has now taken root in it, with ideological nonsense about right and other trash of the kind so familiar to the democrats and the French socialists.
Quite apart from what has been set out so far, it was in general a mistake to make a fuss about so-called distribution and to put the main emphasis on it.

Any distribution whatever of the means of consumption is only a consequence of the distribution of the conditions of production themselves. The capitalist mode of production, for example, rests on the fact that the material conditions of production are in the hands of non-workers in the form of property in capital and property in land, while the masses are owners only of the personal condition of production, labour-power. If the elements of production are distributed in this way, then the present-day distribution of the means of consumption follows of its own accord. If the material conditions of production are the co-operative property of the workers themselves, then a distribution of the means of consumption different from the present one follows in just the same way. Vulgar socialism (and from it in turn a section of the democrats) has taken over from the bourgeois economists the practice of considering and treating distribution as independent of the mode of production, and hence of presenting socialism as turning principally on distribution. Now that the real relation has long since been made clear, why go backwards again?
4. “The emancipation of labour must be the work of the working class, in relation to which all other classes are only one reactionary mass.”

The first strophe is taken from the opening words of the Rules of the International, but “improved”. There it says: “The emancipation of the working class must be the act of the workers themselves”; here, on the other hand, “the working class” has to emancipate — what? “Labour”. Let him understand who can.
By way of compensation, the antistrophe is a Lassallean quotation of the purest water: “in relation to which (the working class) all other classes form only one reactionary mass”.

In the Communist Manifesto it says: “Of all the classes that stand opposed to the bourgeoisie today, the proletariat alone is a really revolutionary class. The other classes decay and go under with large-scale industry; the proletariat is its most characteristic product.”

The bourgeoisie is conceived here as a revolutionary class — as the bearer of large-scale industry — in relation to the feudal lords and the middle estates, who want to hold on to all the social positions that are the creation of obsolete modes of production. They do not, therefore, form together with the bourgeoisie only one reactionary mass.

On the other hand, the proletariat is revolutionary in relation to the bourgeoisie because, having itself grown up on the ground of large-scale industry, it strives to strip production of the capitalist character that the bourgeoisie seeks to perpetuate. But the Manifesto adds that the “middle estates … (become) revolutionary … in view of their impending transfer into the proletariat”.

From this point of view, therefore, it is once again nonsense to say that they, “together with the bourgeoisie”, and with the feudal lords into the bargain, “form only one reactionary mass” in relation to the working class.

At the last elections, did anyone call out to the artisans, small manufacturers, etc., and peasants: “In relation to us you, together with the bourgeois and the feudal lords, form only one reactionary mass”?

Lassalle knew the Communist Manifesto by heart, as his faithful know the sacred writings of which he is the author. If he falsified it so grossly, then, it was only in order to put a good face on his alliance with the absolutist and feudal opponents against the bourgeoisie.

In the above paragraph, moreover, his oracular saying is dragged in by the hair, without any connection at all with the botched quotation from the Rules of the International. So here it is simply an impertinence, and one by no means displeasing to Herr Bismarck, one of those cheap pieces of loutishness that the Marat of Berlin goes in for.

5. “The working class strives for its emancipation first of all within the framework of the present-day national state, conscious that the necessary result of its efforts, which are common to the workers of all civilised countries, will be the international brotherhood of peoples.”

Lassalle, in contrast to the Communist Manifesto and to all earlier socialism, had conceived the workers' movement from the narrowest national standpoint. He is being followed in this — and that after the work of the International!

It goes without saying that, in order to be able to fight at all, the working class must organise itself at home as a class, and that its own country is the immediate arena of its struggle. To that extent its class struggle is national, not in its content but, as the Communist Manifesto says, “in its form”. But the “framework of the present-day national state”, for instance the German Empire, itself stands in its turn economically “within the framework of the world market” and politically “within the framework of the system of states”. Any merchant you care to name knows that German trade is at the same time foreign trade, and the greatness of Herr Bismarck consists precisely in his own kind of international policy.

And to what does the German workers' party reduce its internationalism? To the consciousness that the result of its efforts “will be the international brotherhood of peoples” — a phrase borrowed from the bourgeois League of Peace and Freedom, which is meant to pass as an equivalent for the international brotherhood of the working classes in their common struggle against the ruling classes and their governments. So not a word about the international functions of the German working class! And this is how it is supposed to stand up to its own bourgeoisie — which is already linked in brotherhood against it with the bourgeois of all other countries — and to Herr Bismarck's international policy of conspiracy!

In fact, the internationalism professed by the programme stands even infinitely below that of the Free Trade party. That party too asserts that the result of its efforts will be “the international brotherhood of peoples”. But it also does something to make trade international, and by no means contents itself with the consciousness that all peoples carry on trade at home.

The international activity of the working classes does not in any way depend on the existence of the International Working Men's Association. That was only the first attempt to create a central organ for this activity; an attempt which, through the impetus it gave, has had a lasting success, but which in its first historical form could no longer be carried on after the fall of the Paris Commune.
Bismarck's Norddeutsche was entirely right when it announced, to its master's satisfaction, that in its new programme the German workers' party had forsworn internationalism.
II

“Starting from these principles, the German workers' party strives by all legal means for the free state — and — socialist society; the abolition of the wage system together with the iron law of wages — and — exploitation in every form; the elimination of all social and political inequality.”
I shall come back to the “free state” later.

So, in future, the German workers' party has got to believe in Lassalle's “iron law of wages”! So that it shall not be lost, the nonsense is committed of speaking of the “abolition of the wage system” (it should read: the system of wage labour) “together with the iron law of wages”. If I abolish wage labour, then naturally I abolish its laws as well, whether they are “iron” or spongy. But Lassalle's attack on wage labour turns almost entirely on this so-called law. To prove, therefore, that the Lassallean sect has won, the “wage system” must be abolished “together with the iron law of wages” and not without it.

Of the “iron law of wages”, as is well known, nothing belongs to Lassalle except the word “iron”, borrowed from Goethe's “eternal, iron, great laws”. The word iron is a label by which the true believers recognise one another. But if I take the law with Lassalle's stamp on it, and therefore in his sense, I must also take it with his justification for it. And what is that? As Lange showed shortly after Lassalle's death: the Malthusian theory of population (preached by Lange himself). But if this theory is correct, then once again I cannot abolish the law, even if I abolish wage labour a hundred times over, because the law then governs not only the system of wage labour but every social system. Basing themselves precisely on this, the economists have been proving for fifty years and more that socialism cannot abolish poverty rooted in nature, but can only make it general, spread it evenly over the whole surface of society!
But all this is not the main point. Quite apart from the false Lassallean version of the law, the truly outrageous step backwards consists in this:

Since Lassalle's death the scientific insight has made its way in our party that wages are not what they appear to be, namely the value or price of labour, but only a disguised form of the value or price of labour-power. With this, the whole bourgeois conception of wages until then, as well as all the criticism directed against it until then, was thrown overboard once and for all, and it was made clear that the wage worker has permission to work for his own life, that is, to live, only in so far as he works for a certain time for nothing for the capitalist (and hence also for those who share in consuming the surplus value along with him); that the whole capitalist system of production turns on prolonging this unpaid labour, by extending the working day or by developing productivity, by putting greater strain on labour-power, etc.; that the system of wage labour is therefore a system of slavery, and indeed of a slavery which becomes harsher in proportion as the social productive forces of labour develop, whether the worker receives better or worse payment. And after this insight has made more and more headway in our party, there is a return to Lassalle's dogmas, although people must by now have known that Lassalle did not know what wages were, but, following in the wake of the bourgeois economists, took the appearance for the essence of the thing. It is as if, among slaves who had at last got behind the secret of slavery and broken out in rebellion, a slave still caught up in obsolete notions were to write on the programme of the rebellion: Slavery must be abolished because the feeding of slaves in the system of slavery cannot exceed a certain low maximum! Does not the mere fact that the representatives of our party were capable of so monstrous an attack on the insight that has spread among the mass of the party prove by itself with what criminal levity, with what lack of conscience, they went to work in drawing up the compromise programme!

Instead of the vague closing phrase of the paragraph, “the elimination of all social and political inequality”, it should have been said that with the abolition of class distinctions all the social and political inequality arising from them disappears of itself.
III

“In order to pave the way for the solution of the social question, the German workers' party demands the establishment of producers' co-operatives with state aid under the democratic control of the working people. The producers' co-operatives are to be called into being for industry and agriculture on such a scale that the socialist organisation of the total labour will arise from them.”

After the Lassallean “iron law of wages”, the prophet's remedy! The way to it is “paved” in a worthy manner! In place of the class struggle that actually exists there steps a newspaper scribbler's phrase — “the social question”, for whose “solution” the way is being “paved”. Instead of arising from the revolutionary process of transformation of society, the “socialist organisation of the total labour” “arises” from the “state aid” that the state gives to producers' co-operatives which it, not the worker, “calls into being”. This is worthy of Lassalle's fancy that one can build a new society with state loans just as one can build a new railway!
From a remnant of shame, “state aid” is placed “under the democratic control of the working people”.
In the first place, the majority of the “working people” in Germany consists of peasants and not of proletarians.

Secondly, “democratic” in plain German means “ruled by the people”. But what is “the control of the working people, ruled by the people” supposed to mean? And above all in the case of a working people which, through these very demands that it puts to the state, declares its full awareness that it is neither in power nor ripe for power!

It is superfluous to go here into a critique of the recipe prescribed by Buchez in the reign of Louis Philippe, in opposition to the French socialists, and taken up by the reactionary workers of the Atelier. Nor does the chief offence lie in having written this specific miracle cure into the programme, but in going back altogether from the standpoint of a class movement to that of a sectarian movement.

That the workers want to establish the conditions for co-operative production on a social scale, and to begin with in their own country, that is, on a national scale, means only that they are working to overthrow the present conditions of production, and it has nothing in common with founding co-operative societies with state aid! As for the present co-operative societies, they are of value only in so far as they are the independent creations of the workers, protected neither by the governments nor by the bourgeois.
IV
I come now to the democratic section.
A. The free basis of the state
To begin with, according to II, the German workers' party strives for “the free state”.
Free state — what is that?

It is by no means the aim of workers who have rid themselves of the narrow mentality of humble subjects to make the state “free”. In the German Empire the “state” is almost as “free” as in Russia. Freedom consists in converting the state from an organ standing above society into one completely subordinate to it, and today, too, the forms of the state are more free or less free to the extent that they restrict the “freedom of the state”.

The German workers' party — at least if it adopts this programme as its own — shows that its socialist ideas do not go even skin-deep, in that, instead of treating existing society (and the same holds for any future one) as the basis of the existing state (or of the future state, for future society), it treats the state rather as an independent entity possessing its own “intellectual, moral and free foundations”.

And then there is the gross misuse the programme makes of the words “present-day state” and “present-day society”, and the still grosser misunderstanding it creates about the state to which it addresses its demands!

“Present-day society” is capitalist society, which exists in all civilised countries, more or less free of medieval admixture, more or less modified by the particular historical development of each country, more or less developed. The “present-day state”, on the other hand, changes with each country's frontier. It is different in the Prusso-German Empire from what it is in Switzerland, different in England from what it is in the United States. “The present-day state” is therefore a fiction.

Nevertheless, the different states of the different civilised countries, in spite of the motley variety of their forms, all have this in common: they stand on the ground of modern bourgeois society, only one more and another less developed in the capitalist sense. They therefore also have certain essential features in common. In this sense one can speak of the “present-day state system”, in contrast to the future, in which its present root, bourgeois society, will have died away.

The question then arises: what transformation will the state system undergo in a communist society? In other words, what social functions will remain there that are analogous to the present functions of the state? This question can only be answered scientifically, and one gets not a flea's hop nearer to the problem by combining the word “people” with the word “state” a thousand times over.

Between capitalist and communist society lies the period of the revolutionary transformation of the one into the other. To this there corresponds also a political transition period, whose state can be nothing other than the revolutionary dictatorship of the proletariat.
Now the programme has nothing to do either with the latter or with the future state system of communist society.

Its political demands contain nothing beyond the old democratic litany known to the whole world: universal suffrage, direct legislation, popular rights, a people's militia, etc. They are a mere echo of the bourgeois People's Party, of the League of Peace and Freedom. They are all demands which, in so far as they are not exaggerated into fantastic notions, have already been realised. Only the state to which they belong lies not within the borders of the German Empire but in Switzerland, the United States, etc. This sort of “state of the future” is a present-day state, although it exists outside “the framework” of the German Empire.

But one thing has been forgotten. Since the German workers' party expressly declares that it is operating within “the present-day national state”, that is, within its own state, the Prusso-German Empire — otherwise most of its demands would be meaningless, since one demands only what one does not yet have — it ought not to have forgotten the chief thing, namely that all those pretty little things rest on the recognition of the so-called sovereignty of the people, and are therefore in place only in a democratic republic.

Since one has not the courage — and wisely so, for the circumstances call for caution — to demand the democratic republic, as the French workers' programmes did under Louis Philippe and under Louis Napoleon, one should not have resorted to the subterfuge, neither “honest” nor dignified, of demanding things that make sense only in a democratic republic from a state which is nothing but a military despotism, trimmed with parliamentary forms, mixed with a feudal admixture, already influenced by the bourgeoisie, bureaucratically carpentered together and guarded by the police, and of assuring this state into the bargain that one imagines one can force such things on it “by legal means”!

Even vulgar democracy, which sees the millennium in the democratic republic and has no inkling that it is precisely in this last form of state of bourgeois society that the class struggle has to be fought out to a finish — even it towers mountains high above this kind of democratism, which keeps within the bounds of what the police allow and logic does not.

That by “state” is in fact meant the government machine, or the state in so far as it forms a special organism of its own, separated from society by the division of labour, is shown by the very words: “The German workers' party demands as the economic basis of the state: a single progressive income tax, etc.” Taxes are the economic basis of the government machinery and of nothing else. In the state of the future that exists in Switzerland, this demand has been pretty well fulfilled. Income tax presupposes the different sources of income of the different social classes, and hence capitalist society. It is therefore nothing remarkable that the Liverpool Financial Reformers — bourgeois headed by Gladstone's brother — are putting forward the same demand as the programme.
B. The intellectual and moral basis of the state
“The German workers' party demands as the intellectual and moral basis of the state: 1. Universal and equal popular education by the state. Universal compulsory school attendance. Free instruction.”
Equal popular education?

What do people imagine is meant by these words? Is it believed that in present-day society (and it is only with present-day society that one is dealing) education can be equal for all classes? Or is it demanded that the upper classes too shall be compulsorily reduced to the modicum of education — the elementary school — that alone is compatible with the economic conditions not only of the wage workers but of the peasants as well?

“Universal compulsory school attendance. Free instruction.” The former exists in Germany, the latter in Switzerland and the United States, as far as elementary schools are concerned. If in some states of the latter “higher” educational establishments are also “free”, that in fact only means meeting the cost of the education of the upper classes out of the general tax fund. Incidentally, the same holds for the “free administration of justice” demanded under A, 5. Criminal justice is to be had free everywhere; civil justice turns almost exclusively on conflicts over property and so concerns almost exclusively the propertied classes. Are they to conduct their lawsuits at the expense of the national purse?
The paragraph on the schools should at least have demanded technical schools (theoretical and practical) in combination with the elementary school.

Entirely objectionable is “popular education by the state”. Laying down by a general law the funds of the elementary schools, the qualifications of the teaching staff, the branches of instruction, etc., and, as happens in the United States, supervising the fulfilment of these legal requirements by means of state inspectors, is something quite different from appointing the state as educator of the people! Government and church should rather be excluded equally from any influence on the school. In the Prusso-German Empire above all (and let no one get out of it with the lame excuse that one is speaking of a “state of the future”; we have seen how matters stand with that), it is, on the contrary, the state that needs a very rough education by the people.

But the whole programme, for all its democratic jingle, is tainted through and through by the Lassallean sect's servile belief in the state, or, what is no better, by a democratic faith in miracles; or rather it is a compromise between these two kinds of faith in miracles, both equally remote from socialism.
“Freedom of science”, runs a clause of the Prussian constitution. Why, then, have it here?

“Freedom of conscience”! If, at this time of the Kulturkampf, one wanted to remind liberalism of its old catchwords, it could surely only have been done in this form: Everyone must be able to relieve his religious needs, like his bodily ones, without the police poking their noses in. But the workers' party ought at any rate to have taken this opportunity to express its awareness that bourgeois “freedom of conscience” is nothing but the toleration of every possible kind of religious freedom of conscience, and that for its part it seeks rather to free consciences from the spectre of religion. But it chooses not to go beyond the “bourgeois” level.
I have now come to the end, for the appendix that follows in the programme is not a characteristic part of it. I can therefore be very brief here.
“2. Normal working day.”
In no other country has a workers' party confined itself to so vague a demand; they have always fixed the length of the working day that they regard as normal under the given circumstances.
“3. Restriction of women's labour and prohibition of child labour.”

The standardisation of the working day must already include the restriction of women's labour, in so far as this relates to the length, breaks, etc., of the working day; otherwise it can only mean the exclusion of women from branches of industry that are especially unhealthy for the female body or morally objectionable for the female sex. If that is what was meant, it should have been said.
“Prohibition of child labour”!
Here it was absolutely necessary to state the age limit.
A general prohibition of child labour is incompatible with the existence of large-scale industry and is therefore an empty pious wish.

To carry it out — if it were possible — would be reactionary, since, with strict regulation of working time according to the different age groups and other precautionary measures for the protection of children, the early combination of productive labour with education is one of the most powerful means of transforming present-day society.
“4. State supervision of factory, workshop and domestic industry.”

In relation to the Prusso-German state, it should definitely have been demanded that the inspectors be removable only by a court of law; that any worker be able to denounce them to the courts for neglect of duty; and that they must belong to the medical profession.
“5. Regulation of prison labour.”

A petty demand in a general workers' programme. In any case, it should have been stated clearly that the workers have no wish, out of fear of competition, to see ordinary criminals treated like cattle, and above all no wish to cut them off from their only means of reform, productive labour. That was surely the least one might have expected from socialists.
“6. An effective liability law.”
It should have been said what is meant by an “effective” liability law.

It may be noted in passing that, in speaking of the normal working day, the programme has overlooked the part of factory legislation that concerns health measures and safeguards against danger, etc. The liability law only comes into operation once these regulations have been violated.
In short, this appendix too is distinguished by slipshod drafting.
Dixi et salvavi animam meam. (I have spoken and saved my soul.)
